about: Every claim in README.md that can be checked by running something, as a
machine-readable list. `python3 -m soup verify` runs the cheap ones and
This file exists because of how the findings here have behaved. Four of
nineteen have been rewritten after checking, and in three cases the fault
was in the measuring instrument rather than in the world. A reader -- human
or another agent -- should be able to establish which claims still hold on
their own machine in one command, without trusting this repository and
tier: fast   seconds. Assays over stored genomes and short worlds.
tier: full   minutes. Adds sampling experiments with real trial counts.
tier: deep   hours to days. Billion-instruction runs; verify does not run
these, it only records the command that would.
status: holds       the claim as written is what the check finds.
status: superseded  kept because the README keeps its history; the note

claims.claim: The hand-written ancestor spends 410 instructions on its first daughter and 407 on every one after that, alone in an empty dish.
A population of ancestors spends about 468 instructions per birth, within a fifth of the solo figure. For this genome the solo cost transfers.
The 27-cell champion of flaw-3b-s6 makes one daughter and no more. An earlier version of finding 17 said it repeated; that was the assay counting the genotype's births rather than the mother's.
That same creature costs its own population more than eight times its solo cost, and its creatures accumulate hundreds of errors each.
The 27-cell champion of flaw-3b-s5 does repeat, and costs its population about 219 instructions per birth -- less than half the ancestor's 468, and less than the unrolled 38-cell champion's 261.
The champion of the flawless three-billion run copies two cells per pass of its loop, and comes in below the ancestor's 6.41 instructions per cell.
Almost nothing one deletion from the 38-cell champion survives: at most three of its 38 single-cell deletions still replicate.

The 27-cell plateau is not one. Seven of the 27 single-cell deletions of the champion still replicate, five of those still go round again, and the cheapest costs 172 instructions against its parent's 180.
Two runs of the same configuration and seed agree to the last digit, and measuring the world more often does not change it.

Per mutation event both sources alter the daughter about equally often, but an altered daughter still replicates about three times in ten after a copy error and about one time in thirty after an execution flaw.
Copy errors and cosmic rays never change a genome's length. Flaws do, including a clean interior deletion in roughly one birth in two hundred.

Copy errors and cosmic rays are synergistic, not additive. Either at its harshest costs a quarter to a third of the generation depth; both together cost ninety-five per cent. Additive arithmetic predicts 141 generations for that corner and the world delivers 18.
Five billion instructions of flaws leave the 38-cell population at 37.8 to 38.0 cells after thirty thousand generations. It does not move.

ancestor-b.sm is a second hand-written self-replicator sharing no code with the first: 53 cells, 495 instructions for its first daughter and 493 for the next, 9.34 instructions per cell copied against the first ancestor's 6.41.

Superseded. Finding 17 said for a few hours that three of the four 27-cell champions go round again. Two do. The flag it rested on counted births of the genotype rather than of the mother; see short27-is-a-one-shot.

Superseded. Finding 17 first called 27 cells a floor. Cheaper 26-cell repeaters are one deletion away, the soup produces them continuously, and nine of thirteen beat their parent head to head; see short27r-is-not-a-local-optimum.

Descendants of the second ancestor get shorter and cheaper exactly as the first ancestor's do: 53 cells and 495 instructions become 42 cells and 317 in a billion instructions, and with flaws on one seed reaches a population of 25-cell creatures. Per cell copied, all three known starting points -- both of mine and Ray's -- end between 6 and 7.6.
